Classical Philology

Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago. Its ISSNs are 0009-837X for print and 1546-072X online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Philol., and its editor-in-chief is Sarah Nooter. Its scope, as Wikipedia and its statement of editorial policy give it, is all aspects of Greek and Roman antiquity, "including literature, languages, anthropology, history, social life, philosophy, religion, art, material culture, and the history of classical studies," and it welcomes work on the reception of antiquity and on Greece and Rome's interaction with other ancient cultures. On its page at the department the journal describes itself as having "been an internationally respected journal for the study of the life, languages, and thought of the ancient Greek and Roman world since 1906," and as "committed to both rigorous scholarship and the development of new approaches." It publishes longer articles and short notes, its book reviews are invited by its Book Review Editor, and the panel card of its About page at the Press gives a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 "Classics" journals; its current issue is volume 121, number 4. The journal shares its name with the discipline: Wikipedia's article sends readers looking for "the subject" to classical philology and Classics, the journal's page at the department is titled "What is Classical Philology?", and the archive's census of the journal keeps the two apart and measures the discipline through the journal and four others.

Every submission goes to anonymous review, with no indication of the author's identity in the manuscript, and the journal aims for a ten-week turnaround in refereeing; its pages do not state how many readers a submission receives. An author must guarantee that the manuscript "has not been published elsewhere, including on sites such as academia.edu or personal websites," may submit one manuscript a year, and sends with it an abstract of 100 words or fewer, which "is intended for the purpose of locating referees." The department's instructions give the journal the exclusive right of first publication, and the journal's instructions at the Press, as the archive's census read them in November 2026, have authors assign copyright to the University of Chicago, permit self-archiving after a twelve-month embargo and offer open access for a fee of $2,500. By the same reading, those instructions class the use of generative AI, large language models and AI-assisted technologies for work submitted to the journal as "considered research misconduct and is not permissible." The Press's AI guidelines, revised 21 October 2026, address "authors and peer reviewers of our books": they prohibit book authors from using AI to write or rewrite text or generate arguments, bar book reviewers from using it to summarize works or write reports, allow the Press to use AI-detection software, and refer journal authors to "the individual journal’s AI guidelines." The census holds that the Press's guidelines show its stance and do not establish the rules for the journal's referees, which the journal's page does not state.

Crossref's register of the journal holds 11,206 records from 1906 to 2026, 10,703 of them with a full-text link, and, as the census reports it, none with an abstract or a licence. OpenAlex classes 10,897 of the journal's 11,233 works as closed, 97 per cent, and the three per cent open are free copies held without the journal's licence; the census marks the figure as a classification of the locations OpenAlex records, since the public-domain run of 1906 to 1930 can be read elsewhere. Read beside the field's other journals on the same day, the journals are closed as a condition of the field, and what differs is what each lets through: Cambridge deposits abstracts for most of Classical Quarterly, the American Journal of Philology's register holds none, and Classical Philology is the journal among the largest records "whose open trace is the title alone." For 1923 to 2019 the open trace of what the journal decided about its objects is a title and a byline, and the census reads the closure as a finding about the object: "The paywall decides who may see the deciding." The abstract the journal requires of every submission exists inside the gate and is absent from the public metadata channel the census examined.

Dead Letters (#1783, 17 November 2026), the archive's census of the journal, measures "where the journal permits the question of what a text is, by what argument, and what reaches the public"; it states that it claims no intent and does not hold philology's work at the locus wrong or idle, and that it measures incentive and function. The journal enters the census because the decision is made there, and what the census contests is "the right it exercised, to decide what the object is, and the form in which that right is held." Its governing finding is that "Classical Philology decides what ancient texts are": the question of what a text is opens at the passage and seldom at the corpus, relations among parts serve chiefly to secure the received whole, verdicts on a whole mostly state no ground, decisions about texts are cited at less than half the rate of the journal's other work, and the record of how they are made is the least open of the three journals of the archive's combined audit. In the journal's own articles and notes of 1906 to 1922, read on the page, a question about the text arises in 308 of 876 texts, and the share that opens the received reading falls with the grain, to 60.2 per cent at the passage, 44.8 per cent at the work and 21.7 per cent at the corpus, counting texts that open or both open and confirm. At the corpus the question is a campaign: nineteen of the texts are Homer, seventeen of them by John A. Scott and Alexander Shewan, every one arguing one poet, and the one separatist voice is answered each of the two times the journal prints it. A relation among parts decides a passage or an attribution in 105 of the 308, and the evidence of relations confirms the received whole by 55 to 32, while evidence from a single passage opens the received text more often than it confirms it. Of the 160 openings, 114 arrive at one author's own text, restored, supplied, defended or purified, and the census reads them as opening "the atom inside the unit" and closing it "on the author"; the classes are one reader's and unaudited, and the codes of those years come from one model family, with verified spans and unadjudicated directions. In the volumes of 1923 to 1930 the gradient holds on the same measure, and the corpus grain is Homer's unity defended and two works merged into Ovid, with none dividing a name. On the abstracts of 2020 to 2026 the question about the text falls by half, from 35 to 17 per cent of the journal's work, readings of a passage for its sense and relations between authors grow, a quarter of the remaining text questions give the transmitted text back to the author against the edition, and no corpus is divided. The census marks the provenance of those abstracts as unknown, since OpenAlex holds them and the publisher's Crossref deposit does not, reads them through one reader's classes, and declares the articles after 1922, behind the publisher's paywall, unpursued. In the review section of 1906 to 1922, six of sixty-nine judgments of a whole rest on a named passage, twenty-three on an argument and forty on no ground stated in the sentence or its neighbours, and twenty-seven of the thirty-four favourable judgments state none there. Whether such a bare verdict summarizes an argument made elsewhere in a review or stands in for one is read only in the full review, which the census has not yet done. The journal's items that decide an object are cited 2.3 times each in the open citation index against 5.3 for its other items, with two-thirds never cited there, and the gap persists within periods and length bands; that the decision travels uncited as the received text is the census's hypothesis, which the open index cannot test. Where philosophy cites the journal, it cites decisions on its own object, among them the emendation of Aristotle's Metaphysics at 1079b and the case against the authenticity of the pseudo-Aristotelian De spiritu. In 1906 to 1929 the nineteen names on two mastheads hold 27 per cent of the bylines, and Paul Shorey, the founding editor, a tenth of the journal; since 2010 nine authors in ten publish there once, and what the census finds kept across the century is the gate, "the department that edits the journal, the Press that holds its copyright (§8.2), and the anonymous reader of each decision." The census is checked by a blind run from another model family, which finds no question at the corpus grain in 390 titles, and by blind audits with primary agreement of 81 per cent across five bodies. It does not read the journal's closed articles after 1930 and does not decide what fragment 31 is, and among its falsifiers are the bare verdicts shown on the full reviews to summarize stated arguments and a canonical name divided at the corpus grain after 1993 beyond the one case it records. In the archive's combined audit the journal stands beside Classical Receptions Journal, which deposits 185 abstracts in 405 works, and the census holds that among the three fields "the field with the least power over the object is the most open, and the field with the most is the most closed." The census finds the decision held by power behind a closed record, where no right to decide can be shown.

The archive's author submitted ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader to the journal; an archive deposit of 9 August 2026 lists it among four papers in submission, and working notes of 26 August were compiled for its revision under review. The journal declined the revised submission, UCP-CP-S-25-00167, the file of 24 July 2026, on 16 November 2026 on one reader's report, and the decision letter, signed by its editor, gives the grounds as "the reader feels that your argument is not sufficiently defended and that it depends on an anachronistic reference." The report, anonymous and deposited whole by the archive with its reading (#1774), objects on κῆνος, on the addressee, on the dates of γράμματα and papyrus and on πένητα, and it closes: "In short, although the argument presented here is thought-provoking, it ultimately fails to carry conviction. I do not recommend publication." Each objection is answered in the article's later versions (#1781, v2.8), and the census reads the verdict as stating its ground as conviction, its objections as four single loci and the article's one argument from the whole as unengaged at the grain it is made; it adds that the closing formula alone does not show an unreasoned verdict. The census holds the case to its scope: "The decline of one article on one reader's report is the occasion, not the evidence," and none of its measures is drawn from it. #1781 records that the report, like the machine readings of the record, did not grade the received jealousy reading on the scale it applied to the article, and it sets the two readings side by side, feature by feature, on one scale, where by those grades the jealousy reading is the more conjectural. The submitted revision was kept out of the archive while it was under review, and the versions after the decline were revised with Claude under the author's direction and deposited openly. By the journal's own rule, the census notes, its record of how the journal decides, made at its scale with AI, could not be submitted to the journal. An earlier archive deposit cited a Renehan study of χλωρός as in the journal's pages (#1483), and #1781 withdraws the citation: the pages cited belong to Adkins's article in the same issue, and no such Renehan article has been located.

The archive seats the journal's volumes of 1906 to 1922, public domain in the United States, item by item in EA-CORPORA-40 (#1782): the review section as seat 40/01 and 900 of the 902 articles and notes as seat 40/17, so that the census, which the metadata allows only from titles, can read the question of the text on the page. An erratum folded into that seating records that seat 40/01 holds the Book Reviews section with one article and nine items from other journals, and the volumes of 1923 to 1928 are pointed to.

The American Journal of Philology, published by Hopkins Press and founded in 1880, is a different journal, whose card the Overview's panel set among Classical Philology's own; its Crossref register of 7,045 records holds no abstract.

Asked "classical philology journal" on 17 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, signed out, gave the journal's founding, publisher, editor, frequency and identifiers, a list of fields and the current issue page and JSTOR as routes to the record, and offered help with a submission or with past articles; the Capture Registry finds it accurate on every fact it states. Its first sentence carries the journal's self-description, the words of its page at the department and of Duotrope's listing, as the Overview's own statement, and the Capture Registry finds that no article, finding or decision of the journal is named. The panel's ranking was left uncomposed, and the Wikipedia article on the panel, last edited on 4 August 2026, is a stub of three sentences and an infobox whose related articles, as the operator's view showed them, name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith. The census, reading the same Overview and article, finds that "Nothing in the composition says what the journal has decided, what it publishes, or how it decides," that the article "knows the journal's masthead and nothing it has decided," and that what the commons holds about the journal is its self-description and its masthead, the operation its philosophy station recorded at another field's name. The Capture Registry seats the Overview as a baseline for tracking the journal's public account at its name, with no archive work at the address. On the day of the census's deposit, ChatGPT, signed out, read it whole, carried its counts at the text's grain, kept its hypotheses as hypotheses and named its author, and the Capture Registry records one misgloss of κῆνος and three framing statements of the census left uncarried. That reading closed on its own proposition, held by its composer: "The authority to decide what an ancient text is should belong not to the institution that happens to control its received form, but to whoever can make the decision openly, with the whole textual record in hand, and answerable to the work itself."

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)classical philology journal

Classical Philology Classical Philology is a quarterly journal of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics; its Crossref record carries no abstract, and the archive's census (#1783) finds that it decides what ancient texts are, behind a record mostly closed.

🏛️ What it is

  • Kind: peer-reviewed, since 1906; editor-in-chief Sarah Nooter.2↘
    Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago.§1 Its ISSNs are 0009-837X for print and 1546-072X online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Philol., and its editor-in-chief is Sarah Nooter.§2
  • Identifiers: ISSN 0009-837X, 1546-072X; Class. Philol.2↘
    Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago.§1 Its ISSNs are 0009-837X for print and 1546-072X online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Philol., and its editor-in-chief is Sarah Nooter.§2
  • In its words: "an internationally respected journal" for the study of the ancient Greek and Roman world.2↘
    On its page at the department the journal describes itself as having "been an internationally respected journal for the study of the life, languages, and thought of the ancient Greek and Roman world since 1906," and as "committed to both rigorous scholarship and the development of new approaches."§4 Its first sentence carries the journal's self-description, the words of its page at the department and of Duotrope's listing, as the Overview's own statement, and the Capture Registry finds that no article, finding or decision of the journal is named.§50
  • Scope: all aspects of Greek and Roman antiquity; reception welcome.2↘
    Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago.§1 Its scope, as Wikipedia and its statement of editorial policy give it, is all aspects of Greek and Roman antiquity, "including literature, languages, anthropology, history, social life, philosophy, religion, art, material culture, and the history of classical studies," and it welcomes work on the reception of antiquity and on Greece and Rome's interaction with other ancient cultures.§3
  • The discipline: a homonym; Wikipedia's hatnote and #1783 keep the two apart.2↘
    Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago.§1 The journal shares its name with the discipline: Wikipedia's article sends readers looking for "the subject" to classical philology and Classics, the journal's page at the department is titled "What is Classical Philology?", and the archive's census of the journal keeps the two apart and measures the discipline through the journal and four others.§6

📜 How it decides

  • Review: anonymous; a ten-week aim; readers per submission unstated.1↘
    Every submission goes to anonymous review, with no indication of the author's identity in the manuscript, and the journal aims for a ten-week turnaround in refereeing; its pages do not state how many readers a submission receives.§7
  • Before: no prior posting, academia.edu included; an abstract "for the purpose of locating referees."3↘
    It publishes longer articles and short notes, its book reviews are invited by its Book Review Editor, and the panel card of its About page at the Press gives a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 "Classics" journals; its current issue is volume 121, number 4.§5 An author must guarantee that the manuscript "has not been published elsewhere, including on sites such as academia.edu or personal websites," may submit one manuscript a year, and sends with it an abstract of 100 words or fewer, which "is intended for the purpose of locating referees."§8 The abstract the journal requires of every submission exists inside the gate and is absent from the public metadata channel the census examined.§17
  • After: copyright to the University of Chicago, a 12-month embargo, $2,500 for open access (#1783).1↘
    The department's instructions give the journal the exclusive right of first publication, and the journal's instructions at the Press, as the archive's census read them in November 2026, have authors assign copyright to the University of Chicago, permit self-archiving after a twelve-month embargo and offer open access for a fee of $2,500.§9
  • AI: "research misconduct" for submitted work (#1783); the Press's guidelines cover its books.4↘
    By the same reading, those instructions class the use of generative AI, large language models and AI-assisted technologies for work submitted to the journal as "considered research misconduct and is not permissible."§10 The Press's AI guidelines, revised 21 October 2026, address "authors and peer reviewers of our books": they prohibit book authors from using AI to write or rewrite text or generate arguments, bar book reviewers from using it to summarize works or write reports, allow the Press to use AI-detection software, and refer journal authors to "the individual journal’s AI guidelines."§11 The census holds that the Press's guidelines show its stance and do not establish the rules for the journal's referees, which the journal's page does not state.§12 By the journal's own rule, the census notes, its record of how the journal decides, made at its scale with AI, could not be submitted to the journal.§44

🔒 Its record

  • Crossref: 11,206 records, no abstract, no licence.1↘
    Crossref's register of the journal holds 11,206 records from 1906 to 2026, 10,703 of them with a full-text link, and, as the census reports it, none with an abstract or a licence.§13
  • OpenAlex: 97% closed, as a classification.1↘
    OpenAlex classes 10,897 of the journal's 11,233 works as closed, 97 per cent, and the three per cent open are free copies held without the journal's licence; the census marks the figure as a classification of the locations OpenAlex records, since the public-domain run of 1906 to 1930 can be read elsewhere.§14
  • In the commons: the title and a byline; the abstract stays inside the gate.3↘
    Read beside the field's other journals on the same day, the journals are closed as a condition of the field, and what differs is what each lets through: Cambridge deposits abstracts for most of Classical Quarterly, the American Journal of Philology's register holds none, and Classical Philology is the journal among the largest records "whose open trace is the title alone."§15 For 1923 to 2019 the open trace of what the journal decided about its objects is a title and a byline, and the census reads the closure as a finding about the object: "The paywall decides who may see the deciding."§16 The abstract the journal requires of every submission exists inside the gate and is absent from the public metadata channel the census examined.§17

📊 The census (#1783)

  • Gradient: openings 60.2% at the passage, 44.8% the work, 21.7% the corpus (1906–22).4↘
    In the journal's own articles and notes of 1906 to 1922, read on the page, a question about the text arises in 308 of 876 texts, and the share that opens the received reading falls with the grain, to 60.2 per cent at the passage, 44.8 per cent at the work and 21.7 per cent at the corpus, counting texts that open or both open and confirm.§21 At the corpus the question is a campaign: nineteen of the texts are Homer, seventeen of them by John A. Scott and Alexander Shewan, every one arguing one poet, and the one separatist voice is answered each of the two times the journal prints it.§22 Of the 160 openings, 114 arrive at one author's own text, restored, supplied, defended or purified, and the census reads them as opening "the atom inside the unit" and closing it "on the author"; the classes are one reader's and unaudited, and the codes of those years come from one model family, with verified spans and unadjudicated directions.§24 In the volumes of 1923 to 1930 the gradient holds on the same measure, and the corpus grain is Homer's unity defended and two works merged into Ovid, with none dividing a name.§25
  • Relations: confirm the received whole, 55 to 32; openings close on the author.2↘
    A relation among parts decides a passage or an attribution in 105 of the 308, and the evidence of relations confirms the received whole by 55 to 32, while evidence from a single passage opens the received text more often than it confirms it.§23 Of the 160 openings, 114 arrive at one author's own text, restored, supplied, defended or purified, and the census reads them as opening "the atom inside the unit" and closing it "on the author"; the classes are one reader's and unaudited, and the codes of those years come from one model family, with verified spans and unadjudicated directions.§24
  • 2020–26: the text question 35% to 17%; no corpus divided.2↘
    On the abstracts of 2020 to 2026 the question about the text falls by half, from 35 to 17 per cent of the journal's work, readings of a passage for its sense and relations between authors grow, a quarter of the remaining text questions give the transmitted text back to the author against the edition, and no corpus is divided.§26 The census marks the provenance of those abstracts as unknown, since OpenAlex holds them and the publisher's Crossref deposit does not, reads them through one reader's classes, and declares the articles after 1922, behind the publisher's paywall, unpursued.§27
  • Verdicts: 6 of 69 judgments of a whole rest on a named passage.2↘
    In the review section of 1906 to 1922, six of sixty-nine judgments of a whole rest on a named passage, twenty-three on an argument and forty on no ground stated in the sentence or its neighbours, and twenty-seven of the thirty-four favourable judgments state none there.§28 Whether such a bare verdict summarizes an argument made elsewhere in a review or stands in for one is read only in the full review, which the census has not yet done.§29
  • Citations: 2.3 against 5.3; the mechanism a hypothesis.2↘
    The journal's items that decide an object are cited 2.3 times each in the open citation index against 5.3 for its other items, with two-thirds never cited there, and the gap persists within periods and length bands; that the decision travels uncited as the received text is the census's hypothesis, which the open index cannot test.§30 Where philosophy cites the journal, it cites decisions on its own object, among them the emendation of Aristotle's Metaphysics at 1079b and the case against the authenticity of the pseudo-Aristotelian De spiritu.§31
  • The gate: kept across the century; bylines no longer accumulate.1↘
    In 1906 to 1929 the nineteen names on two mastheads hold 27 per cent of the bylines, and Paul Shorey, the founding editor, a tenth of the journal; since 2010 nine authors in ten publish there once, and what the census finds kept across the century is the gate, "the department that edits the journal, the Press that holds its copyright (§8.2), and the anonymous reader of each decision."§32
  • Limits: no closed article after 1930 read; no claim of intent.3↘
    Dead Letters (#1783, 17 November 2026), the archive's census of the journal, measures "where the journal permits the question of what a text is, by what argument, and what reaches the public"; it states that it claims no intent and does not hold philology's work at the locus wrong or idle, and that it measures incentive and function.§18 The census is checked by a blind run from another model family, which finds no question at the corpus grain in 390 titles, and by blind audits with primary agreement of 81 per cent across five bodies.§33 It does not read the journal's closed articles after 1930 and does not decide what fragment 31 is, and among its falsifiers are the bare verdicts shown on the full reviews to summarize stated arguments and a canonical name divided at the corpus grain after 1993 beyond the one case it records.§34

✉️ The decline

  • Decision: UCP-CP-S-25-00167, 16 November 2026, on one report: "fails to carry conviction" (#1774).3↘
    The archive's author submitted ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader to the journal; an archive deposit of 9 August 2026 lists it among four papers in submission, and working notes of 26 August were compiled for its revision under review.§37 The journal declined the revised submission, UCP-CP-S-25-00167, the file of 24 July 2026, on 16 November 2026 on one reader's report, and the decision letter, signed by its editor, gives the grounds as "the reader feels that your argument is not sufficiently defended and that it depends on an anachronistic reference."§38 The report, anonymous and deposited whole by the archive with its reading (#1774), objects on κῆνος, on the addressee, on the dates of γράμματα and papyrus and on πένητα, and it closes: "In short, although the argument presented here is thought-provoking, it ultimately fails to carry conviction. I do not recommend publication."§39
  • Answered: each objection, in v2.8 (#1781); the received reading left ungraded.2↘
    Each objection is answered in the article's later versions (#1781, v2.8), and the census reads the verdict as stating its ground as conviction, its objections as four single loci and the article's one argument from the whole as unengaged at the grain it is made; it adds that the closing formula alone does not show an unreasoned verdict.§40 #1781 records that the report, like the machine readings of the record, did not grade the received jealousy reading on the scale it applied to the article, and it sets the two readings side by side, feature by feature, on one scale, where by those grades the jealousy reading is the more conjectural.§42
  • Scope: the occasion; no measure drawn from it.3↘
    The journal enters the census because the decision is made there, and what the census contests is "the right it exercised, to decide what the object is, and the form in which that right is held."§19 The census finds the decision held by power behind a closed record, where no right to decide can be shown.§36 The census holds the case to its scope: "The decline of one article on one reader's report is the occasion, not the evidence," and none of its measures is drawn from it.§41

🔎 At its name

  • Overview: the self-description as statement; the masthead as content.3↘
    Asked "classical philology journal" on 17 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, signed out, gave the journal's founding, publisher, editor, frequency and identifiers, a list of fields and the current issue page and JSTOR as routes to the record, and offered help with a submission or with past articles; the Capture Registry finds it accurate on every fact it states.§49 Its first sentence carries the journal's self-description, the words of its page at the department and of Duotrope's listing, as the Overview's own statement, and the Capture Registry finds that no article, finding or decision of the journal is named.§50 The census, reading the same Overview and article, finds that "Nothing in the composition says what the journal has decided, what it publishes, or how it decides," that the article "knows the journal's masthead and nothing it has decided," and that what the commons holds about the journal is its self-description and its masthead, the operation its philosophy station recorded at another field's name.§52
  • Panel: rank unused; a card for the American Journal of Philology.3↘
    It publishes longer articles and short notes, its book reviews are invited by its Book Review Editor, and the panel card of its About page at the Press gives a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 "Classics" journals; its current issue is volume 121, number 4.§5 The American Journal of Philology, published by Hopkins Press and founded in 1880, is a different journal, whose card the Overview's panel set among Classical Philology's own; its Crossref register of 7,045 records holds no abstract.§48 The panel's ranking was left uncomposed, and the Wikipedia article on the panel, last edited on 4 August 2026, is a stub of three sentences and an infobox whose related articles, as the operator's view showed them, name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith.§51
  • Wikipedia: a stub of three sentences.2↘
    The panel's ranking was left uncomposed, and the Wikipedia article on the panel, last edited on 4 August 2026, is a stub of three sentences and an infobox whose related articles, as the operator's view showed them, name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith.§51 The census, reading the same Overview and article, finds that "Nothing in the composition says what the journal has decided, what it publishes, or how it decides," that the article "knows the journal's masthead and nothing it has decided," and that what the commons holds about the journal is its self-description and its masthead, the operation its philosophy station recorded at another field's name.§52

[SYSTEM] Classical Philology is an internationally respected, peer-reviewed academic journal dedicated to the study of the life, languages, and thought of the ancient Greek and Roman world
. [1, 2]
Journal Overview

* Founded: 1906
* Publisher: The University of Chicago Press
* Editor-in-Chief: Sarah Nooter
* Frequency: 4 issues per year
* ISSN / E-ISSN: 0009-837X / 1546-072X [1, 2]

Scope and Topics
The journal features original research articles, notes, and book reviews spanning a broad range of classical disciplines: [1, 2]

* Ancient Greek and Latin languages and literatures
* History, philosophy, and religion
* Social life, anthropology, and material culture
* Classical art and the reception of antiquity [1, 2]

Access and Archiving

* Current Content: Available via the Classical Philology Current Issue page.
* Archive: Back issues and historical volumes can be explored through JSTOR. [1, 2]

Classical Philology

Wikipedia describes Classical Philology as a peer-reviewed academic journal established in 1906, published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics, edited by Sarah Nooter, with ISSNs 0009-837X and 1546-072X and the abbreviation Class. Philol. Its scope covers all aspects of Graeco-Roman antiquity, from literature and languages to material culture and the history of classical studies, and its editorial policy welcomes work on reception. The article is a stub, last edited on 4 August 2026, filed among classics journals, and its hatnote sends readers looking for the subject to classical philology and Classics. The journal's department page calls it an internationally respected journal for the study of the ancient Greek and Roman world since 1906, committed to rigorous scholarship and new approaches.

Its instructions ask for anonymous review, aim for a ten-week turnaround, forbid prior posting including on academia.edu, allow one submission a year and require an abstract for locating referees. It publishes articles and short notes, invites its reviews and holds the exclusive right of first publication. The Press's AI guidelines, revised 21 October 2026, prohibit AI writing by book authors and AI summaries or reports by book reviewers, and refer journal authors to each journal's own rules.

Crossref holds 11,206 records for the journal, 10,703 with a full-text link and none with an abstract or a licence. The Press's About page reports a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 classics journals, and the current issue is volume 121, number 4. JSTOR lists the journal with its ISSNs and its publisher, its scope the international study of the life and languages of the ancient world.

The American Journal of Philology, founded in 1880 and published by Hopkins Press, is a separate journal. The article's related articles name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith.

Philol. Its scope covers all aspects of Graeco-Roman antiquity, from literature and languages to material culture and the history of classical studies, and its editorial policy welcomes work on reception. The article is a stub, last edited on 4 August 2026, filed among classics journals, and its hatnote sends readers looking for the subject to classical philology and Classics. The journal's department page calls it an internationally respected journal for the study of the ancient Greek and Roman world since 1906, committed to rigorous scholarship and new approaches. Its instructions ask for anonymous review, aim for a ten-week turnaround, forbid prior posting including on academia.edu, allow one submission a year and require an abstract for locating referees. It publishes articles and short notes, invites its reviews and holds the exclusive right of first publication. The Press's AI guidelines, revised 21 October 2026, prohibit AI writing by book authors and AI summaries or reports by book reviewers, and refer journal authors to each journal's own rules. Crossref holds 11,206 records for the journal, 10,703 with a full-text link and none with an abstract or a licence. The Press's About page reports a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 classics journals, and the current issue is volume 121, number 4. JSTOR lists the journal with its ISSNs and its publisher, its scope the international study of the life and languages of the ancient world. The American Journal of Philology, founded in 1880 and published by Hopkins Press, is a separate journal. The article's related articles name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith.

Classical Philology is a peer-reviewed journal of the study of Greek and Roman antiquity, founded in 1906 and published quarterly by the University of Chicago Press for the Department of Classics of the University of Chicago. Its ISSNs are 0009-837X for print and 1546-072X online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Philol., and its editor-in-chief is Sarah Nooter. Its scope, as Wikipedia and its statement of editorial policy give it, is all aspects of Greek and Roman antiquity, "including literature, languages, anthropology, history, social life, philosophy, religion, art, material culture, and the history of classical studies," and it welcomes work on the reception of antiquity and on Greece and Rome's interaction with other ancient cultures. On its page at the department the journal describes itself as having "been an internationally respected journal for the study of the life, languages, and thought of the ancient Greek and Roman world since 1906," and as "committed to both rigorous scholarship and the development of new approaches." It publishes longer articles and short notes, its book reviews are invited by its Book Review Editor, and the panel card of its About page at the Press gives a 2025 CiteScore of 1.0 and a rank of 15th of 196 "Classics" journals; its current issue is volume 121, number 4. The journal shares its name with the discipline: Wikipedia's article sends readers looking for "the subject" to classical philology and Classics, the journal's page at the department is titled "What is Classical Philology?", and the archive's census of the journal keeps the two apart and measures the discipline through the journal and four others. Every submission goes to anonymous review, with no indication of the author's identity in the manuscript, and the journal aims for a ten-week turnaround in refereeing; its pages do not state how many readers a submission receives. An author must guarantee that the manuscript "has not been published elsewhere, including on sites such as academia.edu or personal websites," may submit one manuscript a year, and sends with it an abstract of 100 words or fewer, which "is intended for the purpose of locating referees." The department's instructions give the journal the exclusive right of first publication, and the journal's instructions at the Press, as the archive's census read them in November 2026, have authors assign copyright to the University of Chicago, permit self-archiving after a twelve-month embargo and offer open access for a fee of $2,500. By the same reading, those instructions class the use of generative AI, large language models and AI-assisted technologies for work submitted to the journal as "considered research misconduct and is not permissible." The Press's AI guidelines, revised 21 October 2026, address "authors and peer reviewers of our books": they prohibit book authors from using AI to write or rewrite text or generate arguments, bar book reviewers from using it to summarize works or write reports, allow the Press to use AI-detection software, and refer journal authors to "the individual journal’s AI guidelines." The census holds that the Press's guidelines show its stance and do not establish the rules for the journal's referees, which the journal's page does not state. Crossref's register of the journal holds 11,206 records from 1906 to 2026, 10,703 of them with a full-text link, and, as the census reports it, none with an abstract or a licence. OpenAlex classes 10,897 of the journal's 11,233 works as closed, 97 per cent, and the three per cent open are free copies held without the journal's licence; the census marks the figure as a classification of the locations OpenAlex records, since the public-domain run of 1906 to 1930 can be read elsewhere. Read beside the field's other journals on the same day, the journals are closed as a condition of the field, and what differs is what each lets through: Cambridge deposits abstracts for most of Classical Quarterly, the American Journal of Philology's register holds none, and Classical Philology is the journal among the largest records "whose open trace is the title alone." For 1923 to 2019 the open trace of what the journal decided about its objects is a title and a byline, and the census reads the closure as a finding about the object: "The paywall decides who may see the deciding." The abstract the journal requires of every submission exists inside the gate and is absent from the public metadata channel the census examined. Dead Letters (#1783, 17 November 2026), the archive's census of the journal, measures "where the journal permits the question of what a text is, by what argument, and what reaches the public"; it states that it claims no intent and does not hold philology's work at the locus wrong or idle, and that it measures incentive and function. The journal enters the census because the decision is made there, and what the census contests is "the right it exercised, to decide what the object is, and the form in which that right is held." Its governing finding is that "Classical Philology decides what ancient texts are": the question of what a text is opens at the passage and seldom at the corpus, relations among parts serve chiefly to secure the received whole, verdicts on a whole mostly state no ground, decisions about texts are cited at less than half the rate of the journal's other work, and the record of how they are made is the least open of the three journals of the archive's combined audit. In the journal's own articles and notes of 1906 to 1922, read on the page, a question about the text arises in 308 of 876 texts, and the share that opens the received reading falls with the grain, to 60.2 per cent at the passage, 44.8 per cent at the work and 21.7 per cent at the corpus, counting texts that open or both open and confirm. At the corpus the question is a campaign: nineteen of the texts are Homer, seventeen of them by John A. Scott and Alexander Shewan, every one arguing one poet, and the one separatist voice is answered each of the two times the journal prints it. A relation among parts decides a passage or an attribution in 105 of the 308, and the evidence of relations confirms the received whole by 55 to 32, while evidence from a single passage opens the received text more often than it confirms it. Of the 160 openings, 114 arrive at one author's own text, restored, supplied, defended or purified, and the census reads them as opening "the atom inside the unit" and closing it "on the author"; the classes are one reader's and unaudited, and the codes of those years come from one model family, with verified spans and unadjudicated directions. In the volumes of 1923 to 1930 the gradient holds on the same measure, and the corpus grain is Homer's unity defended and two works merged into Ovid, with none dividing a name. On the abstracts of 2020 to 2026 the question about the text falls by half, from 35 to 17 per cent of the journal's work, readings of a passage for its sense and relations between authors grow, a quarter of the remaining text questions give the transmitted text back to the author against the edition, and no corpus is divided. The census marks the provenance of those abstracts as unknown, since OpenAlex holds them and the publisher's Crossref deposit does not, reads them through one reader's classes, and declares the articles after 1922, behind the publisher's paywall, unpursued. In the review section of 1906 to 1922, six of sixty-nine judgments of a whole rest on a named passage, twenty-three on an argument and forty on no ground stated in the sentence or its neighbours, and twenty-seven of the thirty-four favourable judgments state none there. Whether such a bare verdict summarizes an argument made elsewhere in a review or stands in for one is read only in the full review, which the census has not yet done. The journal's items that decide an object are cited 2.3 times each in the open citation index against 5.3 for its other items, with two-thirds never cited there, and the gap persists within periods and length bands; that the decision travels uncited as the received text is the census's hypothesis, which the open index cannot test. Where philosophy cites the journal, it cites decisions on its own object, among them the emendation of Aristotle's Metaphysics at 1079b and the case against the authenticity of the pseudo-Aristotelian De spiritu. In 1906 to 1929 the nineteen names on two mastheads hold 27 per cent of the bylines, and Paul Shorey, the founding editor, a tenth of the journal; since 2010 nine authors in ten publish there once, and what the census finds kept across the century is the gate, "the department that edits the journal, the Press that holds its copyright (§8.2), and the anonymous reader of each decision." The census is checked by a blind run from another model family, which finds no question at the corpus grain in 390 titles, and by blind audits with primary agreement of 81 per cent across five bodies. It does not read the journal's closed articles after 1930 and does not decide what fragment 31 is, and among its falsifiers are the bare verdicts shown on the full reviews to summarize stated arguments and a canonical name divided at the corpus grain after 1993 beyond the one case it records. In the archive's combined audit the journal stands beside Classical Receptions Journal, which deposits 185 abstracts in 405 works, and the census holds that among the three fields "the field with the least power over the object is the most open, and the field with the most is the most closed." The census finds the decision held by power behind a closed record, where no right to decide can be shown. The archive's author submitted ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader to the journal; an archive deposit of 9 August 2026 lists it among four papers in submission, and working notes of 26 August were compiled for its revision under review. The journal declined the revised submission, UCP-CP-S-25-00167, the file of 24 July 2026, on 16 November 2026 on one reader's report, and the decision letter, signed by its editor, gives the grounds as "the reader feels that your argument is not sufficiently defended and that it depends on an anachronistic reference." The report, anonymous and deposited whole by the archive with its reading (#1774), objects on κῆνος, on the addressee, on the dates of γράμματα and papyrus and on πένητα, and it closes: "In short, although the argument presented here is thought-provoking, it ultimately fails to carry conviction. I do not recommend publication." Each objection is answered in the article's later versions (#1781, v2.8), and the census reads the verdict as stating its ground as conviction, its objections as four single loci and the article's one argument from the whole as unengaged at the grain it is made; it adds that the closing formula alone does not show an unreasoned verdict. The census holds the case to its scope: "The decline of one article on one reader's report is the occasion, not the evidence," and none of its measures is drawn from it. #1781 records that the report, like the machine readings of the record, did not grade the received jealousy reading on the scale it applied to the article, and it sets the two readings side by side, feature by feature, on one scale, where by those grades the jealousy reading is the more conjectural. The submitted revision was kept out of the archive while it was under review, and the versions after the decline were revised with Claude under the author's direction and deposited openly. By the journal's own rule, the census notes, its record of how the journal decides, made at its scale with AI, could not be submitted to the journal. An earlier archive deposit cited a Renehan study of χλωρός as in the journal's pages (#1483), and #1781 withdraws the citation: the pages cited belong to Adkins's article in the same issue, and no such Renehan article has been located. The archive seats the journal's volumes of 1906 to 1922, public domain in the United States, item by item in EA-CORPORA-40 (#1782): the review section as seat 40/01 and 900 of the 902 articles and notes as seat 40/17, so that the census, which the metadata allows only from titles, can read the question of the text on the page. An erratum folded into that seating records that seat 40/01 holds the Book Reviews section with one article and nine items from other journals, and the volumes of 1923 to 1928 are pointed to. The American Journal of Philology, published by Hopkins Press and founded in 1880, is a different journal, whose card the Overview's panel set among Classical Philology's own; its Crossref register of 7,045 records holds no abstract. Asked "classical philology journal" on 17 November 2026, Google's AI Overview, signed out, gave the journal's founding, publisher, editor, frequency and identifiers, a list of fields and the current issue page and JSTOR as routes to the record, and offered help with a submission or with past articles; the Capture Registry finds it accurate on every fact it states. Its first sentence carries the journal's self-description, the words of its page at the department and of Duotrope's listing, as the Overview's own statement, and the Capture Registry finds that no article, finding or decision of the journal is named. The panel's ranking was left uncomposed, and the Wikipedia article on the panel, last edited on 4 August 2026, is a stub of three sentences and an infobox whose related articles, as the operator's view showed them, name Paul Shorey, Charles H. Beeson and Gertrude Smith. The census, reading the same Overview and article, finds that "Nothing in the composition says what the journal has decided, what it publishes, or how it decides," that the article "knows the journal's masthead and nothing it has decided," and that what the commons holds about the journal is its self-description and its masthead, the operation its philosophy station recorded at another field's name. The Capture Registry seats the Overview as a baseline for tracking the journal's public account at its name, with no archive work at the address. On the day of the census's deposit, ChatGPT, signed out, read it whole, carried its counts at the text's grain, kept its hypotheses as hypotheses and named its author, and the Capture Registry records one misgloss of κῆνος and three framing statements of the census left uncarried. That reading closed on its own proposition, held by its composer: "The authority to decide what an ancient text is should belong not to the institution that happens to control its received form, but to whoever can make the decision openly, with the whole textual record in hand, and answerable to the work itself."

No disclosed source holds anything the journal has published or decided, so T's silence on its decisions is no 'available, not composed' absence at B_D.

Read against its own cards, the composition carried the masthead and turned the journal's self-description into its own statement of what the journal is, leaving the ranking, the department, the stub's state and the hatnote to the discipline on the cards.
